title: Most ReLU Networks Admit Identifiable Parameters
claim: Geometric objects such as weighted complexes and bent hyperplanes give a concrete picture of the structure that determines a function's parameters.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, math labels on regions and facets
description: Two side-by-side line drawings with sub-captions. Panel (a) shows a weighted polyhedral complex in the plane. Three black line segments meet at a central vertex and split the plane into three regions. Each region carries a 2x2 matrix label (A_P, A_Q, A_R) for the linear part of the function. Each facet carries a 2-vector weight (c_f(σ1), c_f(σ2), c_f(σ3)), with σ1 = P ∩ Q marked. Panel (b) shows the canonical polyhedral complex. Two black axis-like hyperplanes from first-layer neurons cross at a point. A red bent hyperplane from a second-layer neuron kinks where it crosses them. Regions are labeled with sign sequences such as +++ and −+−. Small arrows mark each hyperplane's positive side. The red bent line draws the eye first. There is no color other than black and red.
caption: Illustration of weighted polyhedral complexes, the canonical polyhedral complex and bent hyperplanes.
abstract: We study the realization map of deep ReLU networks, focusing on when a function determines its parameters up to scaling and permutation. To analyze hidden redundancies beyond these standard symmetries, we introduce a framework based on weighted polyhedral complexes. Our main result shows that for every architecture whose input and hidden layers have width at least two, there exists an open set of identifiable parameters. This implies that the functional dimension of every such architecture is exactly the number of parameters minus the number of hidden neurons. We further show that minimal functional representations can still have non-trivial parameter redundancies. Finally, we establish a generic depth hierarchy, whereby for an open set of parameters the realized function cannot be represented generically by any shallower network.
